parameterNotes.service: the cache whose command thread was held; the latency reading is its GET duration, so the name is the subject rather than a value.
parameterNotes.datastore: the Redis instance the cache talks to; the readings are client-side and instance-wide, and the name says which instance.
parameterNotes.command: the command that held the thread, which is the mechanism; the utilisation series states the hold, and the command says what caused it.
parameterNotes.issuedBy: who issued it, which is what makes the case a stranger's script rather than the application's own traffic; a series cannot carry an author.

groundTruth.rootCauseReason: The session Redis instance runs its commands on a single thread, and an unrelated debugging script issues a KEYS command against it every thirty seconds. KEYS walks the whole keyspace, so each invocation holds that thread for long enough to delay every GET that arrives behind it: the cache's GET latency goes from 0.4ms to 55ms and stays there. The clients are not the bottleneck -- the application-side connection pool utilisation never moves -- and the only thing that changed is a command pattern the instance is not built for.

rootCauseIndicators.description: the instance's single command thread is saturated, which is what a keyspace-wide command does to a single-threaded server
every GET waits behind the command thread, so the latency is a step and not a tail

causalChain.mechanism: a KEYS command issued every thirty seconds holds the single command thread, so every cache GET that arrives behind it waits -- 0.4ms becomes 55ms and stays there

evidenceCheckpoints.description: the GET latency after 21:30, a hundred times the baseline and flat rather than spiky -- which is what a queue behind one thread looks like
the instance reports its single command thread at 100 %, which is the server's own account of the delay
the interval the debugging script issues KEYS at, cited from the case's own parameters -- the command pattern that saturates the thread, and the one fact that changed
the application-side pool never approached its ceiling, which is the sentence that rules the clients out as the bottleneck

remediation.action: stop issuing KEYS against the production instance -- SCAN with a cursor is the command for a keyspace walk -- and run the debugging script against a replica if it needs the keyspace at all

query: Session cache GETs went from 0.4ms to 55ms at 21:30 and stayed there. Which component is the root cause, and why are the clients not it?
